title: Which Assault Charge Fits?
summary: Simple vs. aggravated assault, one question at a time.
note: Helps you find the right statute to read. It does not replace the statute, your prosecutor's guidance or department policy. Not yet verified against official sources.

sbi.q: Did the suspect cause serious bodily injury, or try to?
sbi.help: Serious bodily injury: creates a substantial risk of death, or causes serious permanent disfigurement or long-lasting loss or impairment of a body part or organ.

strang.q: Was a domestic violence victim strangled, or did the suspect try to strangle them?
strang.help: Impeding normal breathing or blood circulation by pressure on the throat or neck, or blocking the nose or mouth.

weapon.q: Was a deadly weapon used to cause, or try to cause, bodily injury?
weapon.help: Anything used or meant to be used in a way that can cause death or serious bodily injury, including an object used that way.

w_mental.q: Did the suspect act purposely or knowingly (not just carelessly)?

point.q: Did the suspect point a firearm at or toward someone, loaded or not?

sig.q: Did the suspect cause significant bodily injury, or try to?
sig.help: Significant bodily injury: temporary loss of the function of a body part or organ, or temporary loss of one of the five senses.

prot.q: Was the victim a protected person doing their job?
prot.help: Police, firefighters, EMS, health care workers, school employees, transit operators, judges, DCP&P workers and others listed in 2C:12-1b(5).

prot_inj.q: Did the protected victim suffer bodily injury?
prot_inj.help: Bodily injury means physical pain, illness or any impairment of physical condition.

bi.q: Did the suspect cause bodily injury, try to, or use a physical threat to make someone fear imminent serious bodily injury?
bi.help: Bodily injury means physical pain, illness or any impairment of physical condition.

mutual.q: Was it a fight or scuffle both sides entered into by mutual consent?

points: Document the injury: hospital, diagnosis, photos, and how long the victim is expected to be impaired.
If the victim is a protected person, note it; it still matters for bail and sentencing.
Domestic relationship? Run the mandatory arrest go-by too.
Look for neck marks, petechiae, voice changes, trouble swallowing; symptoms can show up later.
Get EMS to evaluate. Strangulation injuries can be serious without visible marks.
This is a DV case: mandatory arrest rules and weapon seizure apply.
Recover and photograph the weapon; note how it was used.
Also consider possession of a weapon for an unlawful purpose (2C:39-4).
Fits reckless injury with a deadly weapon.
If the injury was only negligent, it drops to simple assault a(2), a disorderly persons offense.
Pointing at a police officer is a higher grade under a separate paragraph; check the entry.
Recover the firearm or imitation; check permits and also consider weapons charges in 2C:39.
Write down exactly which function or sense was lost and for how long.
Example: knocked unconscious, or a punch that temporarily blinds an eye.
Protected victim plus bodily injury.
Note the victim's role and that they were acting in the line of duty (or because of their status).
A simple assault on a protected victim with no bodily injury.
Note the victim's role and that they were on duty.
Domestic relationship? Simple assault is a DV predicate; run the mandatory arrest go-by.
Consider a complaint-summons unless a warrant is justified.
Both sides agreed to fight. Each may be charged.
Mutual consent is judged by the facts, not just what the parties say afterward.
An offensive touch, shove or threat to do so with purpose to harass fits harassment 2C:33-4(b).
A threat to kill or of a violent crime may be terroristic threats 2C:12-3.
